To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the two main directions of spreading volcanic ashes in Germany, Belgium, Luxemburg and North-Eastern-France can be explained by different wind directions in high atmosphere.

the main spreading directions of recent (primarily allered period) volcanic ashes of “Laacher See“ area can be identified on the base of a quantitative heavy-mineral analysis of recent soils in the FRG, Belgium, Luxemburg and North-East France.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the distribution of volcanic ash from Laacher See in Germany and neighbouring countries.
the distribution of the recent volcanic ashes of the Laacher Lake area in Germany, Belgium, Luxemburg and North-Eastern-France.
the study of recent soils in the area of the Laacher Lake in the Federal Republic Germany, in Belgium, Luxembourg and north-eastern France.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the material of Laacher See tuff (LST) was distributed in a wide region of Germany and in the neighboring countries.

there is a very close connection between the volcanic ashes of the Laacher Lake and the recent soils of Western and Central Europe, which can only be explained by a long-distance transport of volcanic ashes.
the material of this study is composed of several (different) tuffs from the nearby surroundings (up to 50 km) of the Laacher-See area.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the volcanic ash of the Laacher-See area has been spread in two main directions, one to the north-east and one to the south-west, and that the uppermost tuff of this area dominates in all the samples.
the Laacher See tuffs have spread over large areas in the Federal Republic, Belgium, Luxembourg, and north-eastern France.
the heavy mineral spectra of recent soils in the area of the Laacher-See (Federal Republic of Germany, North-Eastern France, Belgium, Luxemburg) show two main directions of dispersion.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the heavy mineral assemblage in soils is not a reliable indicator of provenance, because it can be affected by many processes that occur in soils.

the Laacher See eruption was not a single event but a series of events, and the Laacher See tuff is a composite tuff.
